subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION THAT GOVERNMENT OFFER ASSISTANCE TO CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this morning I heard the news on the radio that Pope John Paul II will be visiting Canada in September 1984. The Pope will be in Canada for ten days, and will be staying three days in my own province, the Province of Quebec. I would like to point out how important this visit is, considering the fact that over 25 per cent of the people of this great country of ours are Catholic, and I also wish to say how pleased I am, as a Member of this House, with the news of this visit. I think it is a great honour that is being bestowed on the Catholics of this country by the leader of 500 million Catholics throughout the world.
I hope that on this occasion, the Government of Canada will offer the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops any help they may require in preparing for this important trip which will be the first time the Pope, who is well loved throughout the world, sets foot on Canadian soil.

subsubtopic: INDEXED SECURITY INVESTMENT PLAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the budget papers the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) filed detail of an Indexed Security Investment Plan, including a detailed ways and means motion, draft amendments to the Income Tax Act, and a full explanation of how the system will work. The Indexed Security Investment Plan is a method whereby those persons who invest in listed securities of public companies can escape paying capital gains tax on the investment where the gain is referrable to inflation.
The scheme proposed is highly bureaucratic and favours only stockbrokers and investors investing in listed securities. It
is small and medium sized businesses that create the new jobs required in the country. This scheme does absolutely nothing for those who invest in small and medium sized businesses to protect them from the unfair gains tax caused by inflation.
The House should form today a special committee to investigate the scheme proposed by the Minister. That committee should determine how it would be possible to provide for small and medium sized businesses the same protection as the Minister proposes to give the big boys in this Indexed Security Investment Plan. Surely if we are to allow those who invest in big businesses to escape tax on inflationary gains, then in the name of all that is fair and all that is decent the same privilege should be extended to those who invest in small and medium sized businesses, businesses that by their very nature cannot be listed on the stock exchange-

subsubtopic: UNITED STATES BISHOPS' PASTORAL LETTER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday the Catholic Bishops of the United States in a special meeting in Chicago produced a new pastoral letter directed specifically toward world disarmament. It is basically a pastoral statement, it is called "The Challenge of Peace- God's Promise and Our Response". In the statement the Bishops condemned all use of nuclear weapons, they questioned the morality of their possession in any country, and they endorsed the concept of a nuclear freeze in the whole world. Basically the Bishops have clearly said "no". Their statement is definitive and precise. It is based upon the fact that the planet which has been given to us to be used by all peoples is in danger of being totally destroyed.
In their statement they have changed one four letter word to another four letter word. The first such word was "curb" arms build-up. It is now "halt" arms build-up. In that light, I remind the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that in the month of December, 1982, the leaders of the six major denominations in Canada gave him almost the same approach and material. I want the Government of Canada to rethink seriously its position on testing the Cruise missile in light of the new moral position proposed by the American Bishops.

subsubtopic: SUPPORT FOR EXTENSION OF MATERNITY BENEFITS TO ADOPTIVE PARENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of many concerned constituents of Kent, I want to join Hon. Members on both sides of the House who have indicated their support for an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act to extend maternity leave benefits to adoptive parents.
This amendment was proposed by the recent Task Force on Unemployment Insurance in the 1980s and is currently receiving intensive evaluation by the federal Government. Unemployment insurance maternity leave benefits are presently extended to employed women during and immediately after their pregnancy not only to allow these individuals the time required to recover and adapt to the physical element of childbirth, but also to give the new parents an opportunity to become acquainted with their new child during his or her first weeks of life.
The requirements are not so different when a child is adopted. All three partners in this new relationship require time and financial assistance to establish a firm base from which the entire family can grow. This assistance and time are unavailable to many working families who have adopted a child, under the current provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. A move by the federal Government to change this situation would be of great service to the social fabric of the Canadian community. Therefore I urge the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) and his officials to continue their valuable discussions with an eye toward presenting a workable proposal in this regard in the near future.

subsubtopic: CHANGES SUGGESTED TO AID OIL AND GAS INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the oil and gas industry in western Canada is on its knees. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), the Deputy Minister of Energy, and most senior officials of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources all know that the National Energy Program is an unmitigated disaster. But does the Government do anything to remedy the situation? No. It will not make the changes it knows should be made because that would be an admission of error. The Government does not have the guts to admit a mistake.
If the Government truly wants the oil and gas industry to contribute to economic recovery it should create an environment which will encourage the industry. Tinkering will never restore confidence. Investors will not play as long as politicians and bureaucrats want to fine tune.
The changes that must be made to the National Energy Program are straightforward. First, prices for all domestic production should be allowed to move to world levels, whether they be up or down. Second, it should eliminate the grant system. Petroleum incentive payments are costly and discriminatory. We are the only country in the world where the Government pays cash for drilling a dry hole. Replace the grant system with an incentive system that is equitable and non-discriminatory. subsubtopic: USE OF FUNDS ON CAMPAIGN AGAINST ACID RAIN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, an article appeared in The Globe and Mail of last Saturday which dealt with the fund-raising practices of the Canadian
May 4, 1983

Wildlife Federation, the largest non-profit charitable organization in the country in the field of conservation. This article quoted Mr. Kenneth Brynaert, executive director of the CWF, as saying that the foundation had collected some $343,228 from the public for the purpose of conducting an anti-acid rain campaign in the United States, while at the same time accepting an $80,000 contract from the federal Department of the Environment for the same purpose. In any event, the sum it spent on the project was less than the contract figure, leaving the foundation more than $350,000 in pocket after a public appeal for funds that were not spent for the purpose for which they were solicited.
This is a situation that reflects badly on other groups in the conservation field and, further, leaves the Government open to the accusation that it is allowing charitable status, with all that that implies from a tax standpoint, to an organization whose of that status is questionable.
As a person vitally concerned with the problem of acid rain, these revelations leave me most upset. Surely the Government owes some answers to this House and the public, who have contributed to the CWF fund drives and who have supported this and other foundations in the acid rain battle and on other conservation issues.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF BONUSES PAID TO QUEBEC EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I would like to comment on the report in this morning's Gazette that secret bonuses of around 4 per cent have been paid to Air Canada executives earning over $45,000 a year. I have three comments only: first, why help only those earning over $45,000? Do other Quebec employees not pay Quebec taxes as well? What is the rationale or principle here?
Second, why pay any bonus when the airline lost $32.6 million last year? Is not the idea of a bonus that it will only be paid in good years?
Third, recently Air Canada laid off 585 ground service workers. I understand they did not get a bonus. They did not get the golden handshake that was given to 600 white collar workers who took early retirement.
At the same time that our airline had a large loss last year, it is arbitrarily selecting a few employees to pay secret bonuses to, selecting other groups to buy into fancy pension plans, and selecting another group to lay off without any such benefit at all.
What sort of management is this? How can such capricious behaviour demand respect anywhere among Canadians? It is as though management feels that the end is nigh and that the privileged classes have to be taken care of before everything goes down the tube.

subsubtopic: CHARTERED BANKS' TREATMENT OF SMALL BUSINESSES AND FARMERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday The New York Times carried a report that Nu-West Group Limited of Calgary, a real estate developer, announced a large loss of 1982, and said that it and its lenders, the banks, have agreed that Nu-West would stop making interest and principal payments on $562 million in loans. The Company has been unable to pay either principal or interest since last fall.
There is an increasing number of small business concerns and farmers who have been pushed into bankruptcy, and their assets, including machinery, livestock and homes, are being taken over by the banks because they cannot meet their loan payments. Would the Minister not agree that the banks are treating their large corporate customers in an entirely different way than they are treating their other customers, including small-businessmen and farmers? Would the Minister consider what steps are necessary or possible to ensure that the banks treat all Canadians in an equally fair and equitable manner?

subsubtopic: CHARTERED BANKS' TREATMENT OF SMALL BUSINESSES AND FARMERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would hope that the banks would pay even more attention to their small borrowers, the small-business men and farmers to whom the Hon. Member has referred. I have made representations myself in that regard. The Prime Minister has done the same. We have certainly had evidence of hundreds of cases where good Members of Parliament, at least on this side of the House, have done their job on behalf of many of their constituents by approaching the institutions concerned and persuading them to help those concerned. I have had numerous reports from Liberal Members of Parliament who have done their job in that regard. I would hope that Members of the NDP would do the same.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO PROTECT INDIVIDUAL BORROWERS
REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO PROTECT INDIVIDUAL BORROWERS
speechtext:
Hon. Members from all Parties have been in touch with the Minister, as I have, concerning home owners who have not been able to make their mortgage payments and have lost their homes, and farmers in every Province who have been pushed into bankruptcy. What I
am saying to the Minister is that the people of Canada who are in difficulty do not just need kind words from the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister. They need some action which would ensure that the banks would treat the ordinary people who are in difficulty in the same way they have treated Nu-West and dozens of other large corporations which now owe $4 billion or more in loans, on which they are paying neither the principal nor the interest. I am asking the Minister whether, instead of just kind words, we will see some legislation which will give protection to ordinary people in this country.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO PROTECT INDIVIDUAL BORROWERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have already stated that I know of hundreds of cases where, indeed, the financial institutions have taken exceptional steps to accommodate some of their smaller clients who are in difficulty. I suggest to my hon. friend that, indeed, if he wants to check, he will find that to be the case.
I am always suspicious of questions coming from the NDP, because the other day when the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap, in a question in the House, said that there had not been any instances in his riding when steps had been taken to help his constituents. I checked this matter with one particular bank, and found that there had been support and help amounting to millions of dollars in the riding of Kamloops-Shuswap, where the Hon. Member said nothing was taking place.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO PROTECT INDIVIDUAL BORROWERS
speechtext: He doesn't know what's going on.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO PROTECT INDIVIDUAL BORROWERS
speechtext: I can only conclude that Hon. Members of the NDP are not following very carefully what is happening in their ridings.

subsubtopic: SOVIET OFFER TO NEGOTIATE ON NUMBER OF NUCLEAR WARHEADS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Yesterday Mr. Andropov of the Soviet Union offered to count warheads as well as missiles at the intermediate range nuclear force talks. This is quite a change from his previous negotiating stance. As the Prime Minister likes to take credit for the policies of the President of the United States when he agrees with them, would he tell the House whether he will be asking the United States to accept this offer as a new bargaining base, or will he suggest that the United States reject it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: SOVIET OFFER TO NEGOTIATE ON NUMBER OF NUCLEAR WARHEADS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was told that the suggestion by Mr. Andropov is a very positive one. I would hope that it would not be rejected, that it would, on the contrary, be examined with great interest and a positive outlook. Thus far, my information is that the United States have not rejected it, but that they want to examine it. Therefore, we are very happy for any movement by either side toward a halt, an eventual reduction in nuclear
May 4, 1983

arms of the INF variety or of the strategic variety. We think it is a step in the right direction.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also directed to the Prime Minister. Mr. Andropov seems to have avoided mentioning what he intends to do with the SS-20s which would be withdrawn from Europe if his offer is accepted. If these weapons are not dismantled but are merely relocated, the site of the relocation is a very important factor. If they are to be relocated just beyond the Urals, they will still be within range of all their present targets in Europe, although technically the missiles would have been withdrawn from Europe.
As reported at page 24114 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said:
-our judgment of how the other track was proceeding would influence us in deciding whether we would go with the Cruise or not.
Does the Prime Minister consider that Mr. Andropov's statement fulfils the requirement?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I believe I answered that by saying that we thought it was a positive gesture. Of course there are difficulties such as that mentioned by the Hon. Member, that if they are withdrawn into the Asian part of the Soviet Union it is still conceivable that they could be targeted on western Europe. Indeed, if they are moved far east in the Soviet Union, they could be targeted on parts of North America. These are obviously questions which must be examined. That is why it is impossible to give an absolute approval or disapproval now, but we think that the proposal is positive in the sense that it suggests a reduction in the number of nuclear warheads.
To those who oppose the possibility in Canada of testing of the Cruise or, indeed, of the possibility of having Euromissiles on the NATO side, I would point out that it is unlikely that Secretary Andropov would have made his December offer for reducing SS-20s, or yesterday's offer for reducing SS-20s, just out of the goodness of his heart. If the Soviets are suggesting a reduction in missiles, it is probably because they are afraid that we will deploy ours. That should therefore be an argument not to lose our cool too soon and not to decide that we will not deploy ours at any cost. On the contrary, there should be a bargaining going on.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: U.S. AND U.S.S.R. OFFERS TO REDUCE NUCLEAR ARSENALS
U.S. AND U.S.S.R. OFFERS TO REDUCE NUCLEAR ARSENALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Prime Minister. Could the Prime Minister indicate to the House the nature of the study which he is making concerning the proposals for nuclear reductions made by both President Reagan and Soviet Leader Andropov related to the exact amount of nuclear weaponry which both sides possess? Will the Canadian Government be prepared to make recommendations to both sides so that true
Oral Questions
progress can be made at the Geneva negotiations on nuclear arms reduction?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: U.S. AND U.S.S.R. OFFERS TO REDUCE NUCLEAR ARSENALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member refers to a study. I do not know of any particular piece of work being done. I know that there is a whole series of studies going on and examinations by the Department of National Defence and by the Department of External Affairs, those two Departments in particular. They are not only being kept informed by the United States but as well, as the Hon. Member knows, the Secretary of State for External Affairs went to Geneva and personally met with the Soviet negotiators. We are obviously in contact all the time with the Soviet ambassador here, and we try to get the Soviets' side of the story in negotiations.
It is with the objective in mind of making a balanced assessment of progress and a will to progress by both sides that we are conducting our policy. Therefore, I cannot refer, once again, to a particular study, but I can assure the Hon. Member that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in particular, has been in contact with both sides to ensure that both sides negotiate seriously and make progress.

subtopic: U.S. AND U.S.S.R. OFFERS TO REDUCE NUCLEAR ARSENALS
speechtext: The purpose of my question was to indicate that the Canadian Government ought to be making recommendations for the Geneva negotiations, based on an informed study.

Madam Speaker, I now want to ask the Prime Minister whether he has taken note of the recent proposal of Chancellor Kohl of West Germany that a Summit meeting be held between President Reagan and Soviet Leader Andropov for the purpose of giving a new impetus to the nuclear arms negotiations in Geneva. Can the Prime Minister confirm whether he raised the subject of a Summit during his recent meeting with President Reagan? Will he now support this proposal in the name of the people all over the world who want, in an even-handed approach, both the Soviet Union and the United States to stop the nuclear arms race?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Yes, Madam Speaker, I can assure the Hon. Member and the House that I did raise the subject of a Summit with President Reagan. I enjoined him-indeed, I pleaded with him-to work toward such a Summit. I think the timing must be left to the United States in terms of not having a Summit in which progress would be negative or counter-productive.
I pointed out to the President of the United States that in our view time was running out, not only politically for him, and perhaps others, but it is running out in terms of the future of humanity so that both sides who are holders of these terrible weapons of destruction be urged on by every group and every member of NATO, at least on our side, to make progress

May 4, 1983
Oral Questions
which at some point might be better made at a Summit than elsewhere. But once again we are monitoring the discussions in Geneva. I repeat the Secretary of State for External Affairs was there. Short of going to Moscow myself, I am not sure what else I could do at this time.
You have been there. We remember.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENTS CONTRACTS-BUY CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Supply and Services. Would the Minister tell us what the Government's policy is with regard to Government contracts which come up for tender? Given the recent budget announcements that Canadian businesses will be steered out of the recession with a helping hand from the Government, will the Minister tell us whether Canadian firms are given priority when tenders are called for contracts involving the Government? Put simply, is it the Government's policy to buy Canadian whenever possible when it comes to contracts with Government Departments?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENTS CONTRACTS-BUY CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased the hon. gentleman has asked that question. I know he is very favourable toward my ministry's policy of attempting to obtain a larger portion of our procurement from Canadian sources with a high Canadian value added.
In terms of fast tracking and in terms of the projects that we have identified within the budget, the Hon. Member will recognize that roughly 49 per cent of them will be administered through my Department, the Department of Supply and Services. Indeed, the projects have been selected as a result of
their high Canadian content and our ability to source the requirements from Canadian firms.

subsubtopic: MR. NYSTROM-ASSISTANCE TO SENIOR CITIZENS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a great honour for me today to present a petition in the House of Commons on behalf of the Saskatchewan Senior Citizens "Action Now" Association. I have had a chance to examine the petition. It contains nearly 5,000 names of people mostly from the Province of Saskatchewan, some of whom 1 recognize. These are senior citizens who are in financial difficulty at this time.
The rules do not allow me to read the entire petition, but I want to point out that it calls for the establishment of a Department of Senior Citizens Affairs, for a substantial increase in pensions, for the means test to be eliminated and also for a pension which is equal to some 70 per cent to 75 per cent of the average industrial wage index in Canada.
I ask my fellow Members of Parliament to examine the petition very carefully and to act upon it because these are the people who built this country of Canada. They deserve better from us who sit in the House of Commons today than they have been given recently.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ISSUANCE OF FIREARMS PROFICIENCY CERTIFICATE
speechtext:
that Bill C-588, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (gun control), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, once a gain it is Wednesday afternoon when we are permitted to put forth Private Members' Bills. In my mind this is the most important part of the entire parliamentary process because it is an opportunity for ordinary Canadians to have their views, expectations and aspirations brought forth for consideration by all of us as Parliamentarians.
Therefore I rise to move second reading of Bill C-588 and its reference to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs so that the Standing Committee can give it detailed study and interested goups of people can present their views on the whole question of gun control.
The Bill specifically relates to the 1978 amendments that have had such a dramatic effect in the minds of many people, particularly those who care about freedom. This is a good opportunity for the public in 1983 to have somne input on a law that was passed in 1978. I hope Members opposite will agree that this is a worthy Bill, will give it second reading and send it to committee. I commend the law officers of the Crown for the excellent assistance they have given me to put this Bill into the proper legal form.
The purpose of the Bill, as I said earlier, is to respond to the honest and legitimate concerns, both practical and philosophical, of ordinary law-abiding Canadians who were and are opposed to the 1978 amendments on gun control. The second purpose is to remove the expensive administrative costs of registering long guns.
Whatever reference is made to guns, certain people think that all guns should be taken away. Others believe we have the right to own a gun, including a hand gun. This Bill in no way affects the existing law as it relates to hand guns.
For many years in this country there has been a system of registration and a rather restricted use of guns. This Bill is not designed to affect that general law. It is designed to respond to those in the west and in the north, because in those rural areas long guns, shotguns and rifles are an everyday part of their lives. Members from downtown Montreal or Toronto have no feeling for this Bill. They have never been in places where a grizzly bear in the backyard is a reality. This is the case for people in my riding and throughout the northern country. This Bill should be given serious consideration. It simplifies the procedure dramatically. For that reason it should be worthy of merit at this time when we have a $30 billion deficit and are trying to find ways to cut down costs.
This Bill will repeal the 1978 amendment which brought in firearms acquisition certificates and the associated registration of guns. It substitutes a requirement anticipated in the 1978 amendments which was never proclaimed. It would have only one condition: before any citizen over 18 can purchase a gun, he or she would need a certificate of proficiency. They would need to know how to care for guns, know the safety aspects as well as the statistics as to how dangerous they can be. As gun owners point out, it is not the gun that causes the problem but the guy who pulls the trigger.
Section 104(2)(c) of the existing law, which was not proclaimed, had a requirement whereby you had to take a course before purchasing a gun. My point is that we do not need all of those other sections in terms of firearms' acquisition certificates, firearms officers across the country and investigations into our individual lives.
May 4, 1983

When you go to buy a gun, a firearms officer inquires into your life. He can tap all sources in Government to find out whether there is something in your background which would make it undesirable for you to own a gun. That is an invasion of privacy to an amazing degree. This Bill states that before you can purchase a gun, you need a certificate from a recognized gun club or wildlife association, that you know about guns and can handle them safely.
This Bill anticipates that such a certificate would be given by a wildlife association or gun club recognized by the provincial Attorney General. The advantage is that it takes the control out of Ottawa and puts it in the hands of provincial Governments which are more responsive in their particular regions. An Attorney General in Alberta or the Yukon would have a set of requirements and would approve recognized clubs in that Province as bona fide clubs. There would be a similar situation in Ontario and Quebec.
As a result of this Bill, I have received many letters from Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario. I have not received one letter of criticism. Many state that this is the first common-sense approach to the whole question of gun control in a long time and they hope it will pass.
I would like to speak briefly about the practical objections of the original Bill C-51; they are well-known to many Members. The first is related to the cost of the firearms officers, the investigations, the applications and the red tape involved in purchasing a gun. There is also red tape in the police administration-for example, the paper work. There is no doubt that gun store owners are greatly hampered. This red tape has increased the cost of their business dramatically. As a result, there is less revenue going into the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Certainly citizens have been inconvenienced, there is no doubt about that.
The irony is that the existing law did not stop the criminal element. In 1977 there were 13,432 offences and in 1981 17,706, an increase of 32 per cent. In 1977 there were 7,500 robberies with firearms. In 1981 there were 9,040. All the evidence shows that ordinary law-abiding citizens have been dramatically inconvenienced. If you, Mr. Speaker, and I go into the field to shoot ducks, you do not have a firearms acquisition certificate and I lend you my gun, you and I are both criminals under this law. However, the real criminals, those who obtain their guns in the underworld or smuggle them across the border, still continue to use their guns to kill our citizens at an ever-increasing rate.
Beyond the practical is the more difficult philsophical question affecting those who have been born and raised in this country. I speak to many people who come from Eastern European countries such as Poland and the Ukraine on an almost daily basis. Poland, for example, has a long history of great power. They are a highly sophisticated people. There are musicians, artists, in fact the whole gamut of what we call civilization. However, after World War II the first thing the Government did was to take away their guns. That was the start of the loss of their freedom.
Criminal Code
They tell me that if individuals cannot have guns, in 10, 20 or 30 years from now the Government will be able to take over. If the ordinary citizen cannot have a gun to protect his home, family and community, it could be that the military would have control. It is hard for native-born Canadians to understand that. We think we are too civilized for that to happen here, but it has happened before. We would be foolish to believe that could not happen in Canada.
These citizens, Mr. Speaker, primarily Canadians from other countries, also point out that the registration of guns has a very large downside in the long run. When we purchase a gun, it must be registered so that any Government knows that you, Mr. Speaker, have 14 guns, I have six guns and our fellow colleagues have so many guns. The Government can come to you at some point in the future and say: "Mr. Speaker, you have 14 guns and we want them. We want your guns or your life." You see, it is an invasion of your privacy.
We do not need that invasion of privacy in this country because surely the objective of gun control is the safe handling of guns. The way to achieve that objective is to make sure that people know how to handle guns rather than have them go through an inquisition to obtain a firearms acquisition certificate and then be able to purchase any number of guns as long as they are registered. Why should the issue not be approached from this other perspective?
People have the right to own guns just as they have the right to own cars. But they have to know how to drive those cars because public safety is at stake; therefore they must take a course to learn how to drive a car properly. I would say that is the route to follow, Mr. Speaker, in gun control.
In conclusion, I want to say that we need this Bill. I am hoping that other Members will let it go through because it will save money, It will meet the legitimate philosophical and practical needs of our fellow citizens, and I think it will be for the good of the country in the long run. Let us have the Bill go to committee so that our fellow Canadians may testify as to what they believe we should do, and then, for a change, let us act on it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ISSUANCE OF FIREARMS PROFICIENCY CERTIFICATE
speechtext:
I am very pleased with this opportunity to take part in the debate and to comment on the suggestion put forward by my hon. colleague.
I am sure Hon. Members will remember-I know I do, because I was a Member of the House at the time-all the controversy about Bill C-51. It was not surprising, if we consider that gun control is a subject on which public opinion is very clearly divided and which gives rise to heated debate.
This is understandable, because the subject is one that is literally a matter of life and death and concerns the very essence of our individual freedoms as Canadian citizens. We have all heard the arguments on gun control before. Positions

May 4, 1983
Criminal Code
go from one extreme to another, from outlawing guns altogether to removing all controls. A gun control system reconciling these extreme positions would necessarily be complex and in itself highly controversial.
The gun control measures tabled in Parliament as part of Bill C-51 and passed by Parliament as part of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1977, have brought about basic changes in Canadian gun control legislation. The Government has introduced a control system which I myself, and I think most of us, will recognize as being effective, and which is based on the principle that guns have a legitimate, sometimes essential and often enviable place in the lives of many Canadians.
Guns have played an important role in Canada's history, from the times of the explorers and frontier days till the present time. Throughout this period, Canada has maintained a tradition of responsibility in the use of firearms, and that is what has led us to avoid extreme solutions, such as registering all firearms or setting up depots for firearms that are not in use. The Government has not changed its position, and this philosophy is reflected in the legislation.
Since the introduction on January 1, 1979 of the Firearms Acquisition Certificate system, it is now clear, I hope, that the system was designed to ensure that there would be as little inconvenience as possible to the responsible person who wishes to own and use guns.
Increasingly, it is being recognized that the measures adopted by the Government have been very helpful to police forces in controlling the irresponsible and criminal use of firearms and thereby reducing the number of homicides, accidents and suicides that occur in Canada every year. The proposals being made by my hon. friend deal directly with this matter, and although the procedures he is suggesting are not those I myself would favour, I think his approach is positive and that it has the same objective we all have, which is to use firearms as they ought to be used and not as a means of violence and destruction.
Mr. Speaker, I am proud of the fact that the Firearms Acquisition Certificate system was introduced unobstrusively and without any real problems, that it was very well accepted by Canadians and that since it became effective, the system, as shown by studies made by independent groups, has helped to contribute, together with other gun control measures, towards reducing the number of homicides, accidents and suicides caused by the use of firearms.
I am sure that on the other side, my Opposition colleague is just as anxious as we are to stop the violence that is so often present in our society. I think his suggestions may be useful.
However, I must say I deeply regret the fact that the Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) is now sponsoring Bill C-588, which would replace our present efficient system with new, untested measures that are less strict and that might destroy the progress we have made in the last four years. I listened carefully to the Hon. Member's
speech, and although the measures he is proposing would not, according to him, have that effect, I am not so sure he is right. He has good ideas, and I realize that if his proposals were to destroy the gains we have made, that is certainly not my hon. colleague's intention.
By substituting for the Fireams Acquisition Certificate system the measures proposed in Bill C-588, we would seriously compromise the effectiveness of Canadian gun control legislation. I am convinced that all Hon. Members will reach the same conclusion after looking at the purpose of the Firearms Acquisition Certificate system and at the very extensive screening measures provided by the system which would no longer be applied once Bill C-588 is passed, as proposed by my colleague in the Official Opposition.
For the information of the House, I shall now review briefly the objectives of our gun control legislation and the specific means provided to attain those objectives.
Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, give the three general objectives of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. They are first of all, to prevent the irresponsible use of firearms, second, to promote and safeguard the sensible possession and use of firearms, and third, to punish and discourage the criminal use of firearms.
I am sure that my colleague opposite will agree that these objectives are valid ones and should be followed. However, 1 submit that the means he is suggesting are not necessarily one we would be willing to support at this point. The firearms acquisition certificate system helps to meet the first two objectives through specific control mechanisms. The provisions concerning this system came into effect on January 1, 1979. Since then, anyone aged at least 16 who wants to acquire a firearm by whatever means must obtain a firearms acquisition certificate. This certificate is valid for five years and allows the individual to acquire an unspecified number of unrestricted long-barrelled guns, such as shotguns and rifles. The certificate is usually issued by the firearms officer of the local police force and provides for extensive screening mechanisms. All this might seem somewhat elementary, but since a few years have now elapsed, I feel it is important to go over the objectives and contents of this legislation which has played a significant role, as my Hon. friend reminded us today in making his suggestions.
A certificate will not be issued if the officer is aware of any fact that could make it desirable in the interests of the safety of others or of the applicant that he not be authorized to acquire firearms. Moreover, the certificate will not be issued if, within five years immediately preceding the date of the application, the applicant has been treated for a mental disorder, whether in a hospital, mental institute or psychiatric clinic or otherwise, and whether or not he was confined to such an institution when his disorder was associated with violence.
May 4, 1983

How can we determine whether the applicant comes under one of these provisions? First of all, in his application, he must indicate whether any one of them applies to him and a penalty is provided for anyone who makes a false statement. Second, all applications are examined by the centralized records service. In addition, all applications are referred to the local police division of the region where the applicant resides. My friend and colleague said earlier that there is a lot of red tape involved and that many provisions seem to delay application of the law, but I believe that those I have just described are essential and that it would be difficult to replace them by other provisions which may expedite matters, but would not meet the objectives of the law. Several important provisions to which I have just referred would be removed with Bill C-588. Under the present system, firearms acquisition certificate is issued by a firearms officer and it is an important provision since it guarantees an effective screening to prevent irresponsible individuals from acquiring firearms. The police has access to some information which is unavailable to others and this enables them to eliminate applicants who could eventually imperil their own lives and those of other people.
Applying for and obtaining a certificate may appear to be a complex exercise at first glance, as my colleague pointed out, but few Canadians are taking exception to the screening process and to what is considered to be troublesome paperwork for law-abiding citizens. However, it has been clearly established that Canadians are quite ready to abide by the law. This does not mean that I do not agree with my colleague that we should try to avoid some procedures which may perhaps seem cumbersome but to the extent that wherever the purpose of the legislation remains valid, we should not, under the pretence of speeding up the system, be prevented from pursuing our priorities which warranted the legislation which came into force in 1979.
We should not forget that in the first year of implementation of that system, well over 250,000 Canadians were granted firearms acquisition certificates, which means somewhow that the problems met by some individuals did not deter a considerable number of Canadians from obtaining it.
More than 629,000 applications were processed in the first three years. Most Canadians have shown willingness to abide by these provisions and, in light of my own experience and of official reports I can say that, considering the number of applications received, there were few problems and criticisms indeed. I presume that my colleague might point to certain instances in his area where the law may have been difficult to apply, I quite agree. Still, I would suggest that the significant aspect is whether the implementation of the law generally has proved useful, reasonable and acceptable. Given the information I have to date, it does seem that the over-all legislation is quite acceptable, even though certain sections might be better amended.
And what about the selection process? Figures show that in the first three years the numbers of rejected applications were
Criminal Code
997, 1,107 and 1,006 respectively. In each of those three years, the rejection rate has been well below 1 per cent of the total number of applications. During that period, appeals were made in 6 to 7 per cent of rejections and, before 1981, 57 per cent of those appeals were submitted by institutions.
Mr. Speaker, it would seem that, generally speaking, the purposes of the legislation have been achieved and, although some applications may have resulted in delays and injustices for people who normally would have been issued those certificates more rapidly, I must conclude that the over-all situation is promising indeed. Again I say that my colleague of the Official Opposition has raised a very challenging and valid issue. I have tried to take a positive approach today and my intention was not to play down the purpose of the Bill which my colleague proposed and perhaps to express a different opinion concerning the various objectives we may share.
I respectfully submit to the House that at this stage it would be premature to consider such major and controversial amendments as those advocated by the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills. Before considering any radical change to our legislation on firearms control, we would be well advised to give the public and the numerous groups of people concerned an opportunity to study the final conclusions of the assessment review and express their opinions and suggestions on appropriate amendments. Again I thank my colleague for this opportunity to air my views on this subject. In the course of the debate, perhaps we will be able to find even more effective formulas to reach the goal we share, namely help Canadians achieve positive rather than negative results with firearms.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak against this Private Member's Bill. I do not believe it is well thought out. I feel some of the provisions in it could actually be quite harmful.
The Bill is intended to substitute a proficiency test for the existing requirements in the Criminal Code for the acquisition of a firearms certificate. What the Hon. Member neglects to do in discussing the matter is to specify what the different conditions are which his new Bill would omit from the controls on possession of a gun. Let me summarize them: "A person who has been convicted within five years immediately preceding the date of his application of an indictable offence; an offence in the commission of which violence is used against another person, threatened or attempted; within five years immediately preceding the date of the application has been treated for a mental disorder in various places; where the disorder for which he was so treated was associated with violence, threatened or attempted; has a history of behaviour occurring within five years immediately preceding the date of

May 4, 1983
Criminal Code
his application which included violence or threatened or attempted violence on the part of the applicant".
These are all rather serious matters. As for the Hon. Member's suggestion that everyone has a right to own a gun even if he has attempted, threatened or used violence in the last five years, well, I suggest that such a person has forfeited the right to possession of a gun. Merely to undergo a proficiency test which shows that the person knows how to use a gun is hardly a substitute for showing responsible behaviour and being a person who can be trusted with a weapon which can be and has been used to kill people.
The Hon. Member also neglected to look carefully into the statistics. He was rather glib in talking about crime increasing. He suggests that the current provisions only cause a nuisance to law-abiding citizens and have not had any effect on crime. This is not so. The Solicitor General's Department commissioned a study to look into the effects of gun control legislation after it was passed in 1977. There is also an independent study by Professor Martin Friedland of the University of Toronto, Faculty of Law. These studies show there has been an impact on violent crime. There has been a reduction in the rate of homicides since introduction of gun control legislation. There has also been a reduction in the number of hunting accidents and in the number of suicides using firearms since the introdu-tion, showing that the legislation has actually been fairly successful.
It is always difficult to pinpoint precisely what caused the reduction in homicides, accidents and suicides because the Provinces have been taking steps in the meantime to improve gun control by virtue of requiring hunting licences. All of the Provinces have gun safety programs. Indeed, six Provinces, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia, have compulsory proficiency tests. New Brunswick is planning to institute these shortly and Newfoundland has a test for one kind of hunting only. So that the Provinces are taking steps and that, combined with better gun control legislation at the federal level, has seen reductions, which of course is what we want. It is actually fortunate that in Canada we do not have a tradition of violence. We have a long tradition of gun control legislation. I suggest these are very healthy signs we want to keep the good traditions we have.
In 1979 less than 60 homicides were committed with hand guns in Canada, only four in Toronto, a City of two million. In comparison, in the City of New York there were 900 hand gun killings. Hand gun homicides were 20 times higher per capita in the United States, and hand gun acquisitions are ten times higher in the U.S. So, the legislation and traditions we have have been extremely healthy and we certainly want to keep them; we do not want to go in the opposite direction. In fact, a Gallup poll indicated that Canadians would be happier to have tighter gun control legislation, and this includes the West where the Hon. Member suggests that people see this as such a great right. Canadians do not recognize this so-called right,
and they are very concerned to keep violence down to the lowest level possible.
Another point I would like to raise, Mr. Speaker, is the provision in the current legislation for proficiency tests which the Hon. Member would make the only requirement for the acquisition of a firearm. There is an existing provision for the Provinces to make a proficiency test compulsory in order to get an acquisition certificate. Thus we can add requirements under the existing legislation which would not be the case under the proposed Bill. No Province so far has instituted this compulsory proficiency test for the acquisition of a firearm, but they are working in that direction. There have been discussions and the Provinces do want to go that way. Certainly they have been going that way with regard to hunting legislation. It would seem to me the best course is to let the current legislation continue to work, that consultation between the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and the Provinces be pursued on the best way to handle proficiency tests which will probably be proclaimed when the Provinces are ready for it. We have effective legislation right now, the problems are not terribly great, but neither should we introduce new problems by slackening legislation which has actually been successful.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am indeed pleased to have the opportunity of speaking on this Bill. The subject matter has been before this House previously and I note in particular that it was the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) who first presented a similar Bill in Bill C-451.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ISSUANCE OF FIREARMS PROFICIENCY CERTIFICATE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I would not want anyone reading Hansard to have even the faintest impression that there is a similarity between Bill C-451 and my Bill, C-588. There is absolutely no similarity at all.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ISSUANCE OF FIREARMS PROFICIENCY CERTIFICATE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, in spite of what the Hon. Member says, it appears to me that the difference between the two Bills is basically terminology, as I have outlined. I suggest that is really the basic change.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this raises in my mind some very serious concerns not only for this House but for the well-being of the Canadian public. First of all, there is a provision in the present legislation, as yet unproclaimed, calling for the applicant for a firearms acquisition certificate to have successfully completed
May 4, 1983

a course or test relating to the safe handling and use of firearms prior to the certificate being issued by the local police. This provision can be implemented upon provincial request. It is necessary to work out the administrative mechanisms to proclaim this provision and we are attempting to do just that with the Provinces at the present time. The House will recall that the whole firearms acquisition certificate system was delayed so we could have extensive consultations with the Provinces on the smooth implementation of this system.
What worries me most is that this Bill requires only that the individual be able to handle a firearm proficiently. The Hon. Member has done away with all the screening procedures presently required. I suggest to him that it is absolutely essential that there be some kind of screening procedure to make sure that people who are habitual criminals or inclined to violence will not have the opportunity of owning a hand gun, or even a rifle for that matter. An individual would be able to obtain a firearm simply by fulfilling the proficiency provision. Obviously in our prisons today there are many people who are proficient at handling firearms and there are many people who would not be using a firearm anyway unless they were proficient in the handling of it. But I suggest there are other criteria to be considered.
Even those not in favour of all aspects of our present legislation do not want those with criminal records involving violence, perhaps a history of violence with firearms, to obtain further weapons. This is what the Hon. Member's Bill proposes to allow. The applicant will not have to complete an application form on which he is questioned about indictable criminal convictions, or treatment for mental disorder for that matter. There will be no requirement for a police check on any individual as long as he can produce a proficiency certificate, regardless of where it was obtained. This, in my view, is not gun control. This is not keeping firearms out of the hands of dangerous persons. This is simply ensuring that the individual knows how to use the firearm. Although this is a very important item in itself, it is certainly not the only one with which we are concerned.
Our jails are filled with people who know how to use firearms, have used them well in the past and would most likely use them well in future if they had the opportunity to do so. The Bill, in fact, means that one of these people can leave jail one day, successfully take his course in handling a firearm the next day, and right after that he can buy a gun. With the possession of the gun he is able to commit crimes if he wishes to do so. Does the House really want to support this kind of legislation? I suggest that it does not?
How does the Hon. Member intend to establish these proficiency courses or test? Are the tests to be uniform in all Provinces or will it be left to each Province to establish its own test, thus making it easier in one Province to obtain a proficiency certificate than in another? There should at least be some standardization, some uniformity in the kind of test
Criminal Code
which would be required before a proficiency licence would be issued to the individual requesting same.
Another question is, what association does the Hon. Member have in mind to issue proficiency certificates? There are just too many questions left unanswered, I suggest, with regard to the proposal of the Hon. Member.
In terms of the present firearms program and its provision for a course or test in the safe handling of firearms, I can tell the House that the federal Government is working with the Provinces and, in particular, the hunter safety co-ordinators to develop a uniform set of guidelines to be used across Canada for courses in the safe handling of firearms when their requirements is proclaimed.
Besides that, the federal Government has begun several other initiatives to promote gun safety. We have produced a series of educational film strips on firearms, use and safety, for northern and remote students in Canada. I note that this is one of the areas with which the Hon. Member was basically concerned, I believe, with regard to the people in the north and those who might also be considered our native people who require long guns. I suggest to the Hon. Member that there is definitely a distinction between the use of long guns and the use of hand guns. Perhaps the Hon. Member's real concern with the legislation totally involves long guns rather than hand guns. If this is so, I think that that kind of distinction should have properly been made; but I did not hear it in his remarks today.
I am pleased to tell the House that the response and reaction to this kit has been most positive and that its use is being expanded by the Provinces in all areas of the country, including urban centres.
In order to bring the gun safety message to those who use firearms but do not necessarily belong to organized groups, we have developed a display card and pamphlets containing the so-called ten commandments on gun safety and information as to where individuals may obtain their firearm safety courses.
This is an important subject and I congratulate the Hon. Member for bringing it forward because it is of continuing interest and concern. However, I do not feel that I can support the legislation proposed by the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills in its present form. With the proposals, the universal principle of keeping guns out of the hands of dangerous individuals is completely destroyed. I would, however, commend to all and sundry that the pamphlet on the so-called ten commandments on gun safety should be widely distributed to everyone. I commend it to the Hon. Member as well. I note that it pertains to safety in all of its aspects. At the beginning it states:
The safe use of your firearm can provide enjoyable sport and recreation. Misuse can injure or kill.
It is the whole intent and purpose of the present Government legislation to see to it that the individual does understand safety and the use of weapons and does, in fact, have proficiency in using a weapon before being licensed in any way, shape

speechtext:
that Bill C-483, an Act to amend the Constitution of Canada (duration of House of Commons), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak on Bill C-483, an Act to amend the Constitution of Canada, in particular its provisions relating to the duration of the House of Commons. The purpose of this Bill is to provide an element of predictability in the calling of federal general elections.
At present there is almost total discretion in the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to choose a time that is convenient to the Government. Under this Bill elections would be held regularly at four-year intervals, except where a term was cut short by the defeat of a Government on a matter of confidence. In the latter event the newly-elected Government would start a fresh four-year mandate. Nothing in this Bill would prevent the Governor General, where a Government lost the confidence of the House of Commons, from calling upon the Opposition to form a new Government in circumstances where the Governor General already has such power.
Through this Bill I would therefore propose that the Constitution of Canada be amended under appropriate procedures in the following manner:
That the term of Parliament be so structured as to allow the House of Commons to continue until dissolved by the Governor General, which shall be not sooner than four years less 40 days, nor later than four years plus 40 days, from the day that the last preceding Parliament was dissolved.
I further propose notwithstanding this set term that:
The Governor General may dissolve a House of Commons at any time if the Government is defeated on a motion for the approval of its budgetary policy, a motion to concur in interim supply or Main Estimates, or a motion expressing loss of confidence in the Government by the House.
This setting of a specific four-year term for Parliament would as a result require a change to the Canada Elections Act. Through this Bill I propose an amendment to the Canada Elections Act, such amendment to enshrine in statute law the constitutional convention that writs for an election are to be issued immediately upon dissolution of Parliament. I propose that writs of election for a general election shall be issued on the day that Parliament is dissolved, and further:
That the Governor in Council shall fix the day on which the poll shall be held at an election which shall not be later than 80 days after the day that the writ of election was issued, and that day shall be named in the writ of election.
I feel this would ensure that general elections and byelections are always held within a reasonable time from the day the writs are issued. I do not have to point out that this is not the case today and refer to the inequities which have occurred. At present, as Hon. Members are well aware, the maximum period for the duration of Parliament is five years.
In our history there has been one exception. During the First World War the Parliament which was assembled in 1911 was extended to 1917 by a special amendment to the British North America Act because of the exceptional circumstances of that war. As there was a section in the British North America Act, there is also a Section in the Canada Act which also allows for the continuation of Parliament. We are all very familiar with the following well-known phrase:
-in time of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection, if such continuation is not opposed by the votes of more than one-third of the House, or the legislative assembly, as the case may be.
This statement has been very controversial in the past. On three occasions Parliament has run its full five-year limit. In 1896 and in 1935 the Governments of the day were each defeated during the following general elections. On the third occasion, in 1945, the Government just barely managed reelection, which is indicative of my point and of this Bill.
The shortest Canadian Parliament, in 1957-58, was technically less than six months, while the Parliament of 1925-26 was slightly more than six months.
Despite the frequency of elections during the decade following 1957, Parliament usually lasts about four years. Our five-year limit for the duration of Parliament is based upon the British model. I am a strong supporter of the British parliamentary system but I believe that a four-year term is an improvement which can be made, much as I dislike criticizing the system of Government because I think we enjoy the best in the world.
In Britain, prior to 1715 there was no limit to the duration of Parliament. In that year the term was set at seven years. With the proclamation of the British Parliament Act in 1911, the duration of Parliament was reduced to five years. Only twice since then has the limit been extended and both times, similar to Canada, because of world wars. The Parliament which began in January, 1911 was extended to eight years; and the Parliament which began in November, 1935 was extended to ten years. Thank heavens for Winston Churchill. The duration of Parliament in Britain, like that in Canada, rarely lasts the specified five years; the British average is between three and four years.
I have provided this information as background to illustrate to the House why I feel the five-year limit to the duration of the Canadian Parliament must be changed. As I have shown, the limit is rarely adhered to and is therefore somewhat meaningless. By practical tradition five years has only been a "not beyond" date and not a fixed and practical limit to the
May 4, 1983

life of a Parliament. The extending of the duration of Parliament in very exceptional circumstances may indeed be acceptable, but on those three occasions when Parliament lasted the full five years it did so for political expediency only. This, I submit, is not a sound or democratic practice. By having what is in essence a "not beyond" but "anything before" date, the democratic process is in the hands of a small group or in many instances in the hands of one man. From what I have seen of this Government in action, that one man frightens me like no one since Adolf Hitler.
As long as there is an alternative time for an election, the Prime Minister is able to pick and choose the time most favourable to him. His own interests become paramount, not those of the nation. This right to select a most appropriate time is of tremendous advantage to a Government-and let there be no mistake-and particularly to its leader. If the situation in the country is not encouraging, to put it mildly, the Government can cling to power, hoping to wait out the storm like right now, unmindful of the harm it continues to inflict upon the nation. What such a Government must realize is that a Government which puts off calling an election until the last possible moment is sure to be criticized during the election campaign for not having the courage to face the voters sooner. Such was the case, as I so well remember, in 1979.
In the situation of a maximum five-year duration it is also very relevant to draw attention to the right of a Government to call an election any time after Parliament convenes. This, too, is a travesty which must not be allowed to continue. Again the Government of the day is permitted to pick and choose issues and circumstances most favourable to itself. There is always the temptation for a Prime Minister to use his power to retain power or to promote Party ends, even though such ends might not be in the public good.
A Prime Minister and a Government, knowing privately when an election will be called, can set about lavishly spending taxpayers' dollars on a host of projects. Have we not seen that? They are known as election goodies for the simple purpose of purchasing goodwill for themselves prior to the election. I am sure we all recall the ringing phrases and the claims of "the just society" and repeatedly being told that "the land is strong". Just as easily we can remember being assured that there would be no wage and price controls.
If specific four-year terms were set for Parliament, the public would realize instantly what was being done at the time it was being done and respond accordingly at the polls when they put that crucial X on their ballots.
The ability to call snap elections, especially in times when the Government's popularity is negligible, is also a powerful tool in the hands of the Prime Minister. When the electorate clearly indicates, primarily through public opinion polls, that it sees the Government as the source of its problems, the Prime Minister can use the threat of an election to keep his Party under control. I think we have seen that displayed dramatically across the way.
Backbenchers on the Government side would be very reluctant to vote against the Party line in the House of Commons or to voice disagreement with Cabinet policy-or
The Constitution
perfidy-if threatened with an election. This is a situation very familiar these days to Members across the way. Many of the 74 Quebec-bloc Members are shuddering right now. How many Government Members feel secure right now? How many would like the election to be called in February next, which would be the case if the four-year term were in place? I am sure they would be shivering in their boots.
A committed 52 per cent of Canadians would like to see a Progressive Conservative Government in office right now. We would welcome an election tomorrow. This Government, knowing just how unpopular it is, is doing everything in its power to try and convince Canadians that it is really doing a bang-up, marvellous job.
The Government is spending the money of Canadians to try and get this false message across. This all bears relevance to a four-year term. The largest advertiser in Canada is not a giant multinational corporation. It is the federal Government telling Canadians how proud they should be of it, and it has to advertise to do it.
It has been estimated that the Government spends about $70 million on advertising a year, and the figure is growing. This is three times the amount spent by the second largest advertiser, can you imagine, General Foods. British parliamentarians have recognized the problems inherent in the system, including the undue advantage given the Government, and there have been many proposals to that Parliament for fixed terms like those of the United States Congress. To my knowledge, this Bill represents the first time a proposal of this nature has been presented to this House.
The system in the United States is a little different from that of Canada and Great Britain in that the nation's leader, the President, is elected by an independent popular vote and does not achieve office by virtue of being the head of the party obtaining the majority of seats in Congress. I do not agree with the system but I do agree with the fixed term.
Those in Congress, in the House of Representatives and in the Senate, as we are all aware, are elected for specific terms. Every two years the entire House of Representatives faces a general election. Senators are elected for six-year terms, but the system is such that only one-third of the terms expire every two years. I am not going to get into Senate reform and an elected Senate, which is long overdue.
Elections for both are held on the first Tuesday following the first Monday in November of even-numbered years. Their term of office begins at noon on January 3 in the year following the election. It is simple, predictable and it works.
The President of the United States is elected for a four-year term, so he is held accountable for his actions at the end of that time. We in Canada would do well seriously to consider placing the same onus of accountability on our Prime Minister in this year of parliamentary reform. We perhaps should consider limiting the term of office of the Canadian Prime Minister to two four-year terms. I hope to introduce a subsequent Bill in this House in the near future to address this issue.

May 4, 1983
The Constitution
The need to place a firm and fixed limit on the duration of Parliament has many other advantages besides limiting those of Government. In keeping with our efforts at parliamentary reform, the specific time limit would provide for a more orderly and practical resolution of the business of Government. It would enable potential and declared candidates from all political parties and those running as independents to plan their election or re-election campaigns in a less costly and more practical manner.
In my own case, I was nominated in March, 1978. At that time it was generally thought the election call was imminent. All the signs pointed to it. However, the election was not called until May of the following year, a period of 14 months; a maiden-in-waiting, if you will!
I am sure such a move would also be welcomed by the Chief Electoral Officer whose duty it is to conduct the general election process. Sometimes the materials are received way ahead of an election, and sometimes not. I understand that some have already been received in my riding. Eliminated would be the chaotic, last minute scramble to implement the gigantic task of enumeration and the vote itself. I am positive the majority of Canadians would support such a cyclical system of Government.
If we wish to restore the public's esteem of Parliament and its respect for the institution, we must think seriously of presenting ourselves to the public on a regular basis for approval or disapproval and not spring emotional surprises on them.
We are the representatives of the public and those we represent must have the opportunity to express their judgment of us at specifically designated intervals. We must not have the right to pick and choose when we will allow Canadians to sit in judgment, particularly if the times chosen are for political purposes and not for the public good.
I am presenting this Bill to the House at this time and by doing so I feel I am giving my clear support to this desirable system of accountability, accountability sadly lacking at this juncture in our history. A four-year term in this Parliament would give the Canadian people some hope after the classic mismanagement of the economy by the present Prime Minister, a Prime Minister supported by a horde of docile, spineless followers who, regardless of the issue or of thoughts for their constituents, rush blindly in his wake saying "Me too".
No matter what the duration of this Parliament, which is the longest in Canadian history with 504 sitting days, I have great faith that the Canadian people will remember the waffling on the budget, the Canadian people being absolutely subjugated. They will remember the pay-offs, the pork-barrelling, the subterfuge, the chicanery, the lack of intestinal fortitude, the deceit and the duplicity of the present regime.
Most Canadians, thank God, have awakened to the fact that the Prime Minister is a man who believes he has the right to rule instead of govern. That sort of thing went out with the divine right of kings. A four-year term would do much to alleviate this sort of action. The character of the left-wing, demagogic Prime Minister is most aptly described by the
statement of Lord Acton when he said "Power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely".
When thinking of a four-year term, I am sure the Canadian people would like to see it in place right now so that in February they could throw these rascals out. This time, regardless of when the election is held, no amount of bluff will help our chameleon Prime Minister. The people will not be fooled by a budget purporting to support free enterprise, by the last minute wooing of President Reagan or by a supposed stand that we saw in the House of Commons today against the U.S.S.R. in the Cruise missile situation. The socialist policies of the Prime Minister are now well known and documented. The lack of honour will be remembered. Voters will remember the fact that there were no resignations from discredited Ministers Lalonde, Chretien and MacEachen over the Gillespie affair or budget leaks. I am sorry, I should not mention names, Mr. Speaker; I apologize.
The "Kings Row" across the way is in reality "Skid Row". It is occupied by a group of derelicts who have forged signatures, approached judges, lobbied for contracts, provided free Air Canada passes, refused to prosecute known enemy agents, allowing our allies to do it for us, elevated cronies to the Senate, been involved in the uranium cartel and then imposed an official silence on the issue. The list is as shameful as it is endless. It is condoned by the leader of this country. Their greed, incompetence and indifference will not be countenanced for much longer.
With the assistance of a public now fed up with the actions of this Government, I am more than confident that our Party as the only alternative will form the next Government. If this Bill passes into law, our Government will be the one charged with the responsibility of putting this four-year time limit into effect. I can assure this House and Canadians in general that we will not be afraid to face them after four years in office.
