speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I came here this afternoon to participate in Private Members' hour, being a great supporter of the right of the Private Member to bring forward ideas into the House of Commons. I looked at the Bill of the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart), C-483. I thought it was a serious proposal and I prepared some remarks in a serious vein. I will make those serious remarks. In listening to the arguments the Hon. Member put forward this afternoon, we can see that he is not particularly serious in trying to get the House to accept this proposal.
As one of those which the Hon. Member calls a spineless, docile Government supporter, I am pleased to stand here and respond to the argument of someone I would consider an intellectual dwarf. The Hon. Member has recited the most superfluous, trite criticisms of the present Government that really reflect the opinions of the lowest common denominator in society, all in support of an argument that I thought at least merited debate. So let us deal with the serious aspects first and the trite and ridiculous later. Mr. Speaker, I hate to respond to someone such as the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. May 4, 1983

Stewart) but, quite frankly, if I do not, someone else must. We must talk this measure out.
I am a member of the Standing Committee on Standing Orders and Procedural reform, and I respect the rights of Hon. Members to bring matters to the House of Commons for serious debate. However, upon hearing the kind of argument put forward this afternoon by the Hon. Member for Simcoe South in support of his Bill, one sometimes wonders whether or not it is worthwhile to give private Members an entire Wednesday afternoon or to enhance Private Members' Hour at all because of the kind of arguments that have been presented.
Let us take the Hon. Member's proposal at face value and deal with it seriously. Then I will respond to the ridiculous things that were said earlier. First, the Bill would provide a situation where every four years on could expect an election. Now, to say that an election would fall on every anniversary date four years hence would, I think, cause some logistical problems. For example, the most recent election was held in February of 1980. This Bill would therefore commit us for a long period of time to having elections during the winter. Now, I suppose the Hon. Member for Simcoe South would propose to allow the Government 40 days, either before or after the anniversary date, in which to call an election, giving the Government three months' leeway. Clause 3 of the Bill would fix a maximum length for any federal election of 80 days.
This Bill would lead to what I would consider to be radical changes in the operation of Canada's current political system. I wonder to what extent short Private Member's Bill should be the avenue for radically changing the parliamentary system. The Hon. Member has said that he is a great student of British parliamentary democracy. One would have to question that statement given the arguments that he has marshalled this afternoon.
Let us look at the specific content of this piece of legislation. The first Clause would repeal Section 50 of the Constitution Act, 1867, by substituting the following:
50. (1) A House of Commons shall continue until dissolved by the Governor General, which shall be not sooner than four years less forty days, nor later than four years plus forty days, from the day that the last preceding Parliament was dissolved.
(2) Notwithstanding subsection (1), the Governor General may dissolve a House of Commons at any time if the Government is defeated on a motion for the approval of its budgetary policy, a motion to concur in interim supply or main estimates, or a motion expressing loss of confidence in the Government by the House.
This amendment to the Constitution Act, 1867, would create a great deal of confusion since it could be interpreted as being in conflict with Section 4 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms which reads:
4. (1) No House of Commons and no legislative assembly shall continue for longer than five years from the date fixed for the return of the writs at a general election of its members.
(2) In time of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection, a House of Commons may be continued by Parliament and a legislative assembly may be continued by the legislature beyond five years if such continuation is not opposed
The Constitution
by the votes of more than one-third of the members of the House of Commons or the legislative assembly, as the case may be.
What will be the limit? Will it be four years, five years? Will the Government be authorized to carry on in time of war or invasion? The Hon. Member does not address that particular concern. He pointed out three examples of Parliament going to its full limit, and I take him at his word as I have not researched it. He said it happened in 1896, 1935, and 1945. He dismisses this by saying that Parliament went to its full limit for political reasons. Well, he did not elaborate on those political reasons. Perhaps I can help him. First, in 1896, the incumbent Conservative Government was fearful of going to the polls and decided to wait for the full five years. In fact, I think it went a little beyond the five years, but it did not do anything wrong. To my understanding, that was not made an issue in the election. There were no charges brought against that particular Government of doing something anti-democratic.
Similarly, it was Mr. Bennett, another Conservative Prime Minister, who went the full limit in 1935. That was not the issue in the election campaign. People did not accuse him of subverting the democratic process.
In 1945, under the Government of Mackenzie King, there was a legitimate reason. The country was still at war and it would have been absolutely irresponsible to have an election take place during the war. There was an election in 1940, just after the war had started, but that was before Canada had fully mobilized and before the attitude of the Canadian society had fully changed to accommodating the war effort. Those are the three examples that he has given.
The Hon. Member goes on to state that he wants to amend Clause 3 of the Bill which, if adopted, would modify Subsection 22.(1) of the Canada Elections Act in such a way that a maximum length for any electoral campaign would be created. Thus we would have in the Canada Elections Act two series of provisions. One would concern the minimum length of a campaign, being Subsection 6(3.1) of the Canada Elections Act which reads:
6.(3.1) Notwithstanding subsection (2) and (3), in no case shall a writ of election be dated or issued on a day that is later than the fiftieth day before polling day.
Another provision would concern the maximum length of a campaign, the proposed Subsection 22(1) which would read:
22.(1) The Governor in Council shall fix the day on which the poll shall be held at any election, which shall be not later than eighty days after the day that the writ of election was issued, and that day shall be named in the writ of election.
Therefore, the combined effect of these two provisions would be that once the writ had been issued, the election should be held no earlier than 50 days and no later than 80 days from the day that the writ was issued.
The global result of these proposed amendments and of the existing provisions of the Canada Elections Act is that a Government would be in a position to call an election any time in four years less forty days from the last election, which election could be held 50 days later, that is, four years plus ten

May 4, 1983
The Constitution
days from the previous election; and four years plus forty days, which election could be held 90 days later, that is, four years plus 130 days from the previous election. This means that the Government would have a real leeway of over four months, leaving a certain amount of discretion with the Prime Minister, something that the Hon. Member for Simcoe South has decried in his speech this afternoon.
Mr. Speaker, let us get down to the real issue. It is really necessary to have set dates for elections? Would that improve our electoral system? There are three countries where elections are held at fixed dates. I am not sure whether the Hon. Member mentioned all three countries, but he did mention the United States. Let us look at France, West Germany and the United States.
In the case of France, the constitution of that country fixes the normal length of a legislative mandate to four years, and elections are held within 60 days of the end of the incumbent's mandate. But the President also has the power to dissolve the National Assembly on special occasion, and he often uses this prerogative. As a matter of fact, only half the number of French legislative elections were called at the end of a four-year mandate.
In the case of West Germany, the Government of that country has found a way to get around the constitution provisions by provoking its own defeat in the Bundestag. We saw this occur last fall. Such a thing would be possible here too since the Prime Minister could arrange to lose a non-confidence motion when he saw fit, or any time within the four-year period.
In the case of the United States to which the Hon. Member referred, the President is, after only two years in office, already back on the campaign trail. We are seeing this happen right now. President Reagan as the incumbent President is supposedly above politics, but he is campaigning day in and day out for his re-election bid later next year. This forces the office of the President to be more responsive to organized lobbies and, in my view, handicaps seriously his margin of manoeuvre. This is one of the main problems with fixed elections. It handicaps the power of the Government and often places the Government at the mercy of organized sectorial interests from inside or outside the country. If federal elections in Canada were held at fixed dates, to be sure some provincial Governments would take advantage of that. We have seen what kind of political games the Provinces have played in the last ten years.
I also have a concern about byelections, one which I do not particularly want to go into at this time.
The Hon. Member is a great admirer of the British parliamentary system, yet from my reading, I do not recall any demand on the part of the Opposition or of the Government in Great Britain to change the system. It is a well established rule in the British parliamentary system that five years is the normal term except where there are extreme circumstances as occured in Great Britain between 1935 and 1945 and as occurred here in Canada from 1911 to 1917 in the case of the war. As I mentioned earlier, it was unnecessary to invoke that
special provision in 1945 because the Government still had its mandate intact, but the ending of the war more or less coincided with the ending of the mandate of Mackenzie King's Government. If we look to the mother of Parliaments, I do not believe that that issue has ever been raised. I do not say categorically, but I do not remember from my reading that this matter is of great concern to the people of Great Britain.
The real reason why the Hon. Member has brought this bill before the House this afternoon has been given by him. His Party has been somewhat frustrated by its inability to gain the favour of the electorate in this country. The Conservatives seeing themselves positioned rather well in the opinion polls, want to change the whole nature of the British and Canadian parliamentary system simply to accommodate their somewhat distasteful lust for power. That is really what it is all about, Mr. Speaker. I would ask the Hon. Member, is this the official position of the Conservative Party? He has stated unequivocally that, should a Conservative Government ever be elected again, this would be the Party policy.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not wish to speak this Bill out. I would like to express some concerns with regards to the proposed legislation. I would like to support some of the concepts which are in it. I found that much of the earlier debate on both sides of the House really deviated from the merits and the disadvantages inherent in the legislation. I feel that is unfortunate. The previous speaker was right in one respect, that is that Private Members' Hour- Private Members' day as it is now becoming-is the only opportunity which private Members have to talk about legislation and concerns which should be dealt with in a legislative
The Constitution
manner. That is a right which is in some ways abused in this House, in that almost every piece of Private Members' legislation is talked out. It is not allowed to go to committee for further action. I find that unfortunate. There is no monopoly on brains and good ideas, and we should have a system in the House of Commons which allows reasonable pieces of private Members' legislation to be studied by appropriate committees of the House, and if there is a consensus within that committee, that it be referred back to the House of Commons for further resolution.
I believe we in the Opposition do ourselves harm when, in the interest of promoting our Bill, we sometimes use all the wrong rhetoric. I can agree with some of the sentiments in that rhetoric, but I feel that to bring it in at this particular time is probably inappropriate and probably did hurt the valuable suggestions in the legislation which the Hon. Member proposed. I believe one of the remarks of the last Liberal speaker points out why I can support this particular Bill. He said, and I will paraphrase, "It maybe inconvenient for the Government in terms of its dealings with lobbying groups and others if it had a fixed date for an election." I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the full concept of when an election should be called is no longer a matter which should just affect the Government and its ability to survive. We in this House should all agree that elections are really the property of the people. Certainly, if various lobbyist groups wanted to speak out on disarmament, on the issue of abortion or on the issue of wage and price controls, they have that right. We may condemn some of the procedures which lobbyist groups use, and from time to time I am sure all of us do that. However, they have the right to speak out during an election, before an election and, of course, after an election. I do not feel, therefore, that is a valid argument on behalf of the Liberal Government.
In terms of an election itself, Canadians should know when the next election is going to be held. They should be in a situation, as well as the Government, to be able to plan for a certain time period for that election. I believe that is reasonable and has much value for Canadian society as a whole. I also believe it has a great advantage for people who would like to run for public office. Many people who would like to seek election are not in a position to run campaigns which may last from 18 months to two years, depending on when the election is finally called. Many people simply cannot afford it. Many people, by the nature of where they work and what they do cannot afford a long-drawn-out period of time prior to an election being called. I am sure that the fact the 1979 election was not called much earlier created economic hardship on some candidates. I certainly remember hearing about candidates who withdrew after nomination. I think there would be great democratic value in knowing exactly when an election was going to take place, not only regarding where you work but because of the cost involved which many people cannot afford. If they have to wait around, as I said, a year or two years for an election to be finally called, that effectively takes

away from the rights of many Canadians to actually take part in an election.
Thirdly, Mr. Speaker, there is another democratic value to a fixed term of the House of Commons. Under the present laws of this land federal Government workers must resign their employment as soon as they indicate they are going to run for nomination. In this country, over 300,000 Canadians are prevented from seeking election unless they resign their jobs.

Leave of absence, I am sorry. The Hon. Conservative Member says there is a difference, certainly technically there is, but being unemployed for two years is an economic harship for people and that is my concern with the present arrangement. We have had situations where people who say they wish to run for a Party nomination are immediately told they must take that leave of absence. The nomination may not take place for five or six months, and the election may not take place for another year or year and a half. So they may be in a position where for two full years they cannot take part in their regular employment. Most Government workers cannot afford that. So I think there is a lot to be gained for the individual.
I think some of the concerns expressed by the Government Member are also legitimate. So I favour this legislation going forward to committee for study. I think many Members on all sides would take part in that study and, if it was possible, come back to the House of Commons with proposals which I think almost all of us, certainly most Canadians, could accept. It would enhance the democratic right of Canadians not only to change the Government when that is their desire, but also to run in elections when that is their desire.
Let me say in closing, Mr. Speaker, that in light of the events which have taken place over the last few days in this House, it is interesting to note that this Private Members' Bill, which changes the Constitution, asks for committee study but does not put a deadline on it and does not insist that the House of Commons pass it after a one-day debate. If you remember the discussions and games-playing to which we have been subjected in the last few days in the House on the important issue of property rights, people want to speed it through the process and they want deadlines for each step of the process. I suggest that sending this Bill to committee for study for whatever length of time is necessary and allowing the House of Commons to debate it for whatever length of time is necessary before we actually pass or fail to pass the legislation, is probably closer to the proper process that we should use for a constitutional amendment. I hope that once we get past the games-playing on the issue of property rights we in this House will sit down and look at a way of dealing with all the proposed amendments which will be made to the Canadian Constitution.
We know that there is an effort to have property rights put into the Constitution. We know that there is still the unresolved issue of what special rights the Province of Quebec should have with regard to the amending formula and other items in the Constitution. We know that we will be asked in the next little while to deal with the issue of aboriginal rights in some proposals which came out of the First Ministers' Conference. Yet we in this House really do not have a process or understanding of how we wish to deal with constitutional amendments. I might add that as a result of some court decisions which are likely to occur over the next few years we can expect to find things in the present Constitution we did not realize we put there, and that the House of Commons may wish to make some corrections. If we decide to make those corrections we should not make them as a result of political expediency or public outcries by one group in society but because we want to make constitutional changes-and we are not talking about changing the whole things as we did two years ago, but rather, of making one or two amendments at a time-and we should think of how we want to do it. This Bill has given me a chance to speak on that, and I think it is something all Members of the House are concerned about and would like to see resolved.

We bring in a good budget, one which the business community says is a good budget, and the Opposition opposes it because there is nothing in it for business. I do not blame Hon. Members opposite for doing that because it is part of the game. However, the problem is the process under which we work. We are constantly in an adversarial position. If I want to say a certain thing concerning a Government Bill, and I am on this side, I will speak to the Government. However, if the Opposition wants the same change, I will not speak to the Opposition and we will have a fight over it. It is this kind of thing which is the most bothersome.
There is something to be said for a fixed term, if it is a fixed term. The Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) spoke of the U.S. fixed term system, but he did not speak of a term in which the Government is defeated and an election is held in a short period of time. It is a fixed term. We speak of that Monday in November every two years. There is no way that Mr. Reagan or the Democrats can be defeated in the House. There are some advantages and disadvantages. However, we must start to consider how we can work things out together.
If any of us were Congressmen or Senators in the United States Government, we would be provided with many more employees than we have in our offices here. However, in such an office, everyone, from the receptionist at the front desk to the Congressman or Senator, would be constantly lobbying. I might lobby someone. The Hon. Member for Simcoe South is a good example. I respect his views. In fact, he is very articulate. I intensely disagree with what he says, but there might be a time when he and I would have to say, "Look, we both want the same thing because it will be good for our constituencies in Thunder Bay-Atikokan and Simcoe South". We might not sit down and sign an agreement, but we would make a deal. That is the way we would work, even though we had quite divergent political philosophies. As I see it, that is impossible to do in this House at this particular time.
A few of us from all sides of the House have been working on the issue of disarmament. We have certain views on it. I know the Hon. Member for Simcoe South does not agree with those views because I have heard him speaking differently in committee. The point is that it is very difficult for a handful of us to work together in an effective way, simply because of our adversarial system. We must vote pretty consistently in accordance with our Party's views. Once in a while Liberals can vote against the Government or an Hon. Member opposite may vote against a Party view, but it does not work very often or very well. It is a system which is different.
I always have some difficulty when someone says to me, "I believe in the British system". I have accepted the British system. Much of its value has been passed through to our parliamentary system. However, since we are on the North American continent, we are always being buffeted by what

happens in the United States. We in Canada are influenced by both sides. Sometimes we have the worst of both worlds, and maybe this is one of them. For instance, concerning the trade union movement, 1 think we have the worst of both sides because the American trade union movement is not nearly as adversarial and works together.
However, in the House we should be working, not toward taking over the American system but, rather, toward adjusting ourselves to an idea which is part British, part American-sort of North American. From the American example we should come to realize that we are not elected by the people of this country to fight against each other. However, that is what happens. Question Period is a show, almost a three-ringed circus. It is always adversarial. A Liberal may ask a question which is either favourable to the Government or to the Opposition, but it does not seem to matter. It does not make sense. It is entirely ridiculous, and I am sure that the Canadian people, seeing this constantly, feel the same way.
Therefore, I believe we can borrow from the United States to some extent. Mind you, when we start borrowing, we must be careful. One of the problems in the American system is that because there is so much lobbying, people believe that politicians always have their fingers in the till. This is rather reinforced by American television programs.
It is very seldom that I have a chance to make a deal with someone from the other side. It simply does not happen. We are labelled as politicians because people feel that we are somewhat like American politicians, but we are not. We do not sit down frequently and decide that the two of us will push something. That type of thing does not go on between Parties in this country, and maybe it is good. We must be very careful that when we borrow, we borrow only the best and that we do it in such a way as to avoid becoming involved in the kind of lobbying which is very bad in the United States.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PUBLICATION OF THE RESULT OF OPINION POLLS
speechtext:
In answer to the Hon. Member, who will undoubtedly have an opportunity to speak on this Bill, we are not prohibiting private polls and we are not prohibiting whatever organizations political Parties feel they need to sense whether a Party is doing well or poorly. What we are saying is that surely, if we want to maintain a responsible democracy, we must as least consider whether it is right to have people, in some cases people who may be well qualified and in other cases people who may not be very professional in their approach, coming out with public opinion polls with a view to publishing them and possibly influencing the election dramatically.
Let me give an example of what happened in the last election. I have here a copy of the Saturday Star, for February 16, 1980, which you will notice, Mr. Speaker, has a well chosen picture of the then Prime Minister of Canada, I would say a picture deliberately included in that edition of the Saturday Star to put the Prime Minister of the nation in the worst possible light. Offsetting that picture is the headline "Liberals lead Gallup by 20 points." The article is written by Peter Regenstreif, copyright, incidentally, by the Toronto Star, 1980. The article commences with:
A solid 20-point lead in the Gallup Poll for the Liberals over the Conservatives points to a probable Liberal majority government after Monday's election.
The truth is that that poll was totally inaccurate. The pollster goes on to say that their records show that 48 per cent of decided voters would be voting Liberal in the ensuing election, 28 per cent would be voting Conservative, and 23 per cent would be voting NDP. In short, the thrust of the poll and the way the article was written was that the Liberals had an unbeatable 20-point lead over the Conservatives, which meant a majority Government.
The fact was that the result in the election showed that the Liberals did not have 48 per cent but 44 per cent of the results and the Conservatives did not have 28 per cent but 33 per cent. While the pollsters portrayed the image of a 20-point gap between the then Government of Canada and the Opposition,
May 4, 1983

on election day the gap in points turned out to be about half of that.
The reason I introduced this Bill, Mr. Speaker, which incidentally was introduced on May 2, three years ago, was that, having lived with the consequence of what the pollsters did in that 1980 election, I felt the time had come when we needed some type of constraint on those that publish polls prior to elections. If you check the repercussions of this type of thing, you will find that most people in this House will tell you that during the 1980 campaign, when meeting people on the doorstep or at public meetings, rather than hearing them say, "Tell us more about the issues or tell us about your leader as opposed to other leaders", the almost inevitable statement was, "It looks like you are going to lose". People told us that they were reading in the paper of a 20-point gap and because of that they would say to us, "Somehow, you cannot make it." The issue became not who should govern this country but who a pollster said was going to win on election day.
Naturally, there are two ways to look at that, both of them wrong. You could say the bandwagon approach is going to favour a person or the Party that looks to be in the lead. That, I suggest, is wrong. Or you could argue exactly the reverse and say that perhaps it will garner a lot of support for the underdog. Taking that scenario, if it is going to be one or the other, I would much sooner be on the bandwagon side than be worrying about getting support for the underdog.

speechtext:
What are the disadvantages of publishing polls right up to election day, as it can be done now? Let me put it succinctly. Think of the effect if it were seriously suggested that a newspaper could take a group of polls-if this could be done-and have the people vote in those polls in some kind of a preliminary election. Let us take the advance polls. What if we published the results of the advance polls prior to election day? Surely there is not a person in this House who would say that that should be done. Why should it not be done? In their heart they would know somehow or other that that is counter to democracy.
How people vote at five advance polls or 100 advance polls should be kept secret to the day the election results are actually tabulated. It would be grossly unfair to have certain advance polls published prior to an election. I do not think there is any doubt about that. If, under the proper scrutiny of the electoral process, we agree that an advance poll should not be published, what on earth is the justification for having people, for a fee or
Canada Elections Act
otherwise, poll 1,000 people or 2,000 people? First of all, it is an invasion of their right to keep how they vote secret by asking them how they are going to vote. Second, what is the justification for taking the totals of, let us say, 2,000 people who have been contacted and issuing the results as if they were indicative of what would happen in the ensuing election?
If we agree that the publishing of an advance poll is wrong-which, after all, would be properly supervised-why should we say that an amateur poll or a professional poll of a random sampling of people is somehow or other okay, is part of freedom of speech or God only knows what, and should not be restrained? We must add to that the fact that any pollster will tell us he can influence the results of a poll by the method he uses in gaining whatever data he needs and how he frames the question. If he wants to be completely fraudulent, he only has to make sure to call the right people who will give the right answers. If all these things are true, I would say the time has come for Parliament at least to consider whether there should be some restriction on this complete, carte blanche publishing of polls literally right up to the day when Canadians are asked to vote.
How often have we heard how people in western Canada resent watching television on election night and seeing the results from eastern Canada being reported? They realize that virtually whatever they have done in the form of voting is almost immaterial. If voters in western Canada feel that way, surely we must ask ourselves why. The reason is that they sense a certain futility. If they feel that way, why is it right to let some amateur or professional group of pollsters tell them in effect the same thing one or two days before?
Some Grits must feel warm all over as they remember the 1980 election and how the polling published in The Toronto Star helped them in the Toronto area. If they want to rise in the House today and defend it, let them also tell us why it was necessary in the Canada Elections Act to prohibit the publication of results in Newfoundland in another time zone in Canada, prior to the polls being closed in that time zone. Obviously it was included because it was felt that if people in British Coumbia knew how the vote had gone in Newfoundland, it would have some influence before the polls closed in British Columbia. If they think that such results should be blacked out on election day and not openly disseminated in British Columbia, why is it all right to have an amateur or professional pollster in effect doing the same thing right up to voting day for whatever devious or other reasons he wants to do it?
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, you might ask, "Yes, but what other country has ever been so bold as to prevent this type of publication?" First, I point out that the Province of British Columbia has a ban on public opinion polls during elections. We have Hon. Members from British Columbia here. Perhaps they could correct me if I am wrong, but I

May 4, 1983
Canada Elections Act
understand that the ban has been in place for almost 30 years. For example, a radio station in Nelson was actually prosecuted in the last election in British Columbia on the basis that its poll contravened the regulations. In France, no polls may be made public during the last week of an election campaign. Australia has a ban, but I am not sure how extensive it is. The Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert)-who said that he would like Hon. Members to know that if he were in the House he would certainly support my Bill-pointed out that this has become quite an issue in that part of the democratic world. Australia feels that a ban on this type of polling is necessary.
We could argue that the publishing of polls is something that may either hurt a Party in one election or help it in the next, but that is not what we are talking about today. We are talking about how we can ensure that our elections are as open, fair and democratic as possible. This entails no preliminary glimpses of how people will vote, because that type of thing becomes self-fulfilling. Those who have the wherewithal to commission polls can commission them as they see fit. They can ask whatever questions they see fit and publish the results as they see fit. I do not think anyone in Canada should have such a right if we want to respect our free democratic system.
Let me point out the types of things a pollster generally will not tell a person making inquiries. I went to see certain officials of the Gallup poll organization and questioned them about the 1980 results. I asked them whether they would reveal who exactly was surveyed, when they were surveyed and where. Other than being given general data, such as between dates and that type of thing, they say that that information is private, and they will not disclose it. If we ask who commissioned the poll or who actually paid them for it, of course we are told that that is private. If we ask whether the interviews that resulted in the data they felt was necessary were conducted by telephone or in person, we may or may not obtain an answer.
I think all these things should be open. If people are to be allowed to continue to publish polls and to show them to whatever advantage or disadvantage they feel will result, surely we should have the right to know who exactly they surveyed, who commissioned it, who paid for the poll and whether the interviews were conducted by telephone or in person.
Professional pollsters have told me that there is a tremendous difference in responses. For example, if they telephone persons, they obtain much more guarded answers than if a professional interviewer sat down with the person, led him up to the question and finally got the answer out of him. The tactics are another matter which I will get into at another time, but we are never furnished with the knowledge of what exactly was the breakdown in terms of number of males polled, number of females polled or the language, how heavily it was oriented to the French, to the English or to any other ethnic group. It was never related, and of course it could not be related, to such things as the total population. Most pollsters will say that they can never be entirely sure of turnout. In complete good faith they may come up with a poll showing
that there will be a vote similar to the one I indicated and if, because of weather or other reasons, a disproportionate number of voters do not turn up, their poll will be automatically inaccurate. They acknowledge the fact that some elections have heavy turnouts and others have comparatively light turnouts. This is something a pollster cannot judge.
The point I am making is that poll results are written up, as they were in The Toronto Star to which I referred, as if they were Gospel on which people can count, but the pollsters tell us that they are accurate, within 4 per cent either way, 95 per cent of the time.
If we cherish our free democratic system, is it right that we allow people to publish polls that can be and literally are admitted to be often inaccurate? That is what we are talking about today.
I would hope that Hon. Members who choose to either talk out this Bill or possibly even speak against it will hesitate to do so. If they believe in democracy in Canada, let them show it by saying that they do not feel there should be this unfair polling of the public leading up to general elections such as happened in 1980.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in the debate on Bill C-555. I begin my remarks by saying to my colleague who has spoken in favour of this Bill that I have too much respect for the intelligent electors of Canada to think they might be swayed by public opinion polls during electoral campaigns. I would remind him that we Quebecers have lived through much more trying times during the referendum campaign when many opinion polls gave contradictory results, yet that did not prevent men and women in Quebec from choosing Canada.

The purpose of Bill C-555 is identical to that in two Bills which have already been debated during the present session. The first one, Bill C-208, was introduced by the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) and debated on June 20, 1980. The second one. Bill C-262, was sponsored by the Hon. Member for Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates) and was debated on November 26, 1981.
One may wonder if all that could be said about this topic has been exhausted. Maybe the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) was absent when the two Bills I mentioned were debated. In any case, for his benefit I would like to repeat some of the comments previously made about this kind of Bill.
The purpose of his proposed amendment to the Canada Elections Act is to prohibit the publication in any manner during the 28 clear days preceding the time that polls are closed in an electoral district in which an election is being held of the result or purported result of a poll of the political opinions of the electors in relation to the election. That is totally unacceptable to me. It is an insult to the intelligence of
May 4, 1983

the Canadian electorate and is a denial of their right to information about themselves.
At first glance it seems rather shocking to have such a proposal to muzzle the press and to deny information to people coming from a Member of the Conservative Party, a Party which has been an energetic champion of the cause of freedom of information. It is interesting that this comes at a time when that Party is out of office and is running 52 per cent in the Gallup poll. It is apparently now in the best interests of this country. However, Members of that Party have not been known for their consistency.
The Hon. Member for Cumberland-Colchester, who is a guiding light in his Party and is trying to assist his Leader in many ways, sponsored Bill C-262 which would prohibit the publication of the results of opinion polls for the entire election period. This may be a little sterner stuff, but I think the real problem of what we are talking about here is that such a Bill really does not treat the Canadian people with much respect. I think it more or less implies that they are like lemmings, that they are like sheep, or like buffalo on the prairies stampeding in one direction, and that direction is whichever way the polls seem to be following.
These fears for the ignorance and gullibility of the electorate for only four weeks do not make much sense to me. I am reminded of the phrase of Franklin D. Roosevelt, Fear nothing but fear itself, and he should have known. In 1936 there was a very famous poll conducted during the U.S. presidential election which showed that Alf Landon would thump Franklin Roosevelt. What in fact happened was that Roosevelt thumped Landon, but the Literary Digest only consulted people who subscribed to the magazine. In the middle of the Depression, the only people who could afford magazine subscriptions were Republicans. Not too long after that, the Literary Digest went out of business.
One can only hope that this House will give this Bill the treatment it so richly deserves, that which was meted out to similar Bills sponsored by the Hon. Member for Cumberland-Colchester and the Hon. Member for Athabasca. Both Bills, Bill C-208 and Bill C-262 respectively, would have prohibited the publication of the results of opinion polls during an election, as is proposed by the Hon. Member for York-Peel at this time; three times in two years.
I might note that a very distinguished Member of this House, no less a distinguished a Member than yourself, Mr. Speaker, said, and I will quote from the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for Tuesday, April 13, 1976, as follows:

That is correct, Mr. Speaker. It is the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis). I apologize for the error. The Hon. Member for Ottawa West said this about the poll, and I quote:
Well, if you were to try to do it on a national basis, you would have the kind of thing where the Detroit paper would do a poll on Canada and publish it in Detroit. The United Kingdom tried to do this and they had it from radio Luxembourg, beamed at the United Kingdom, back and forth. I just do not think it is enforceable. And, while I do not like opinion polls, and while I understand why someone presented the bill, and I wish I could think of a good, ultimate, valid reason why I could achieve the same result, I have to say, deep in my heart,
I think it is wrong.
The point raised in that Committee is a good point. What would happen if a Detroit radio station decided to make public the results of a poll done in Canada? With the cable network and with the techniques we have now, such as the satellite discs, you could have an Atlanta television station broadcast the results of a poll. Are we going to try to stop this? It raises rather horrendous scenes.
You can picture people in eastern Europe huddled beside their radio with the lights out or turned down very low, listening to the "Voice of America" waiting for the police to break down the door. I can think of many movies of the Second World War where the Gestapo would storm in and find somebody with the earphones on. Is that the sort of thing we are going to do? It does not seem very realistic. Once we start muzzling the press and denying the press the right to publish information, where do we stop and, I should say, where do we start?
I understand the motivation behind the Bill presented by the Hon. Member, but it is a very slippery slope. Once you start that sort of process, I do not think there is any guarantee that it will not creep away from us and eat into very fundamental and precious rights. We have always had a free press in this country. A person such as myself on the Liberal side can say that we have enjoyed criticism and all sorts of remarks. We have survived over the years. What would happen if someone would take a poll and then we had a version of a Hyde Park corner in this country? Are you going to extend the Bill to preclude somebody from taking a poll and then standing up on a soapbox to announce it?
Where do you draw the line? The final week ban on publication of poll results involves a clear and obvious abridgement of freedom of expressions. It would restrict individuals, the press, magazines, radio and television for a crucial seven-day period. In the language of journalistic ethics, it would flagrantly and without any question abridge the right of the public to know.
If a late change in public sentiment were under way, this rule would require that knowledge of the change be witheld from the general population. The Bill's sweeping demand, it should be noted, would withold all polls, those accurately reflecting the trend as well as those that might in one way or another be seriously misleading.

Canada Elections Act

I should like to make a brief comment on that, Mr. Speaker. Being from Quebec where I was with the Department of Social Affairs, I know that very often a good many of our departmental policies stemmed from documents drafted after and based on a poll. In my opinion, it is a scientific tool and that is a fact with which well informed people agree today. As to whether all polls are reliable, that is for the client to decide and, in this instance, they are usually sponsored by newspapers during an electoral campaign. I would suggest that the reputation of polling firms has been established, and those which do have some credibility would not jeopardize their future by playing with figures or publishing misleading results. I think that the future of those firms weighs more heavily than the outcome of any election.

Look at the results of the last election. Does anyone think that the results were seriously affected by the polls? Certainly the polls were broadcast far and wide. The voters in western Canada were not very much influenced by them if they believed the polls which indicated that the Liberal Party would do well in eastern Canada. It did not cause a stampede toward the Liberals on the Prairies. Perhaps if anything, it did cause some weakening of our support.
Look at the polls. They did not all say the same thing. The CTV poll, the CBC poll, the Carleton University poll and the Toronto Star poll did not give the same figures, but they all indicated the same trend, and the trend was that the Liberals would win. In fact, the Liberals did win.
What would happen, for example, if we were to ban polls during only the last four weeks of an election campaign? The Ken Taylor Iran incident caused the Tories to think that this might be their salvation, that it might turn things around. Anyone working for the campaign in Toronto during that election who talked to a Conservative worker knows that this incident gave them a real shot in the arm, a real flow of adrenalin. They could hardly wait for the next poll to come out. They felt that somehow a twist or a change in their fortunes would be indicated as a result of the Iranian incident. I must say, however, that they were not responsible for the incident.
Are we to deny the Conservatives the hype or the adrenalin or the good morale that would result from an incident occuring toward the end of an election campaign? Are we to say that if something great happens during the first part of a campaign, the poll will reflect it and the effect may be felt by the electorate and they may go in that direction like lemmings, but that this must not happen in the last four weeks? If that were the case, the Conservatives probably would have asked Ken Taylor to get out of Iran two or three weeks earlier so that there would be time for the polls to reflect that upsurge in their fortunes. This is the ridiculous sort of thing this legislation could trigger.
A point raised by the Hon. Member for Athabasca was the way in which knowledge of the mood of the country would affect the decision of a voter. Somebody who may feel strongly
about a majority Government might like to know if one of the two major Parties had a better chance to form a majority Government than the other. A voter may prefer one of the two major Parties, but actually feel strongly about minority Governments. If he thought the NDP had a chance of holding the balance of power, he would vote for that Party, but only if it would hold the balance of power. I do not see anything wrong with that. That is valid information that should not be denied the electorate.
If anything, in terms of knowledge of politics, elections and the issues, voters are becoming increasingly more sophisticated. I do not think we need to stuff up their ears so they cannot hear information they had a right to hear in the past in case somehow their minds would be tainted and they would go off and do something they would not otherwise do. Mr. Speaker, I believe that in a democratic country such as ours, that is not the kind of thing we must anticipate. As far as I am concerned, the polls can continue.
If a voter was very concerned about having a majority Government and wanted to know which Party had the best chance of forming a majority Government, he could do his own poll. However, the results would only be relevant in his own riding, and the trend in his riding might be going in the opposite direction from that in the rest of the country. In a country that is so spread out, almost 5,000 kilometers long, it is valid for a person in one part of the country to want to know how people in other parts of the country feel.
Our Party will take its chances on the impact that such information will have on the electorate. I do not think that there is a possibility that very many people will place their vote based on the mood of the rest of the country, causing everyone to react in the same way.

Mr. Speaker, the people of Quebec often say that they will not behave like a bunch of sheep. I think that if the leader comes down from the mountain, there is no need for everybody to jump in the water.

The results of the last election, particularly from the area of the country west of Winnipeg, will indicate that. If there was a buffalo stampede in the West, it was not in the direction of the Liberals. It was in the opposite direction, notwithstanding the fact that the direction of the polls was well known.
Another interesting question that arises is the difference between the work of a political commentator, of a syndicated columnist, of a magazine writer and of a pollster. Let us assume a rough equivalence in terms of talent and sensitivity on the part of the three. Are we to say that a political commentator whose columns are carried in newspapers across the country cannot say that he has been talking to many people and finds it pretty clear that the mood of the country is that the Liberals will win this election or the Conservatives will win that election? People respect a columnist's judgment. People believe that if Lynch, Fisher or Fotheringham say something
May 4, 1983

and they have gone up on the mountain and got it in tablets of stone, it must be true. However, one knows that what columnists say is not always true, but if that is the information the people are looking for, they will certainly believe Mr. Lynch or Mr. Fisher. The Conservatives usually believe Mr. Fisher. Are we to say to columnists that they cannot write columns like that in the last four weeks of an election campaign? The Bill does not purport to do that, but what is the difference? Both the columnists and the pollsters give an impression, albeit one is a personal reflection and the other is a scientific impression.
If people are so easily influenced by what authoritative people may say about the mood of the country, rather than read polls by Martin Goldfarb or Peter Regenstreif, they will simply read columns by Charles Lynch or Doug Fisher. We all know how authoritative they are. Their opinions may differ from time to time, but so do the opinions of the pollsters. Opinions are not always identical. That is another problem that can occur if you follow this route.
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude my remarks by saying that in Quebec we believe in taking polls during the election campaign, and that the safeguard provided for the last day only is enough. We believe enough in the freedom of expression and in the judgment of the people of Quebec to allow them to hear the truth right up until the last minute.

The rules of the game and the way polls are taken lead us to believe quite simply that our fellow Canadians can make up their own minds on these issues. Mr. Speaker, I thank the House for its indulgence. I do want to put a few words on record and still allow at least a few minutes to anyone who might want to comment on this particular Bill.
I believe this Bill raises a crucial issue in terms of the whole election and/or referendum procedure because it seeks to divide public opinion on the matter of public property or private property. I listened very carefully to the arguments presented by the Hon. Member for York-Peel. I know there are two sides to the coin, and he has very adequately presented

May 4, 1983
Canada Elections Act
the one side. I would like to perhaps reiterate some of those aspects. In addition, I will illustrate some of the concerns which we in this Party have with regard to the other side of the coin.
One side of the coin follows the premise that a publication of a public opinion poll pertaining to a particular election would subsequently sway opinion. I believe the Hon. Member for York-Peel referred to it as the "bandwagon" effect. As a result, this would have some impact on the election outcome. The second premise which logically flows from this way of thinking is that such swaying of public opinion is manipulative and, of course, this manipulation is bad. Therefore, we have the conclusion drawn by the Hon. Member that there should be a ban on all public opinion polls of electors during an election, and he suggests for a period of 30 days.
On this particular side of the coin, I am prepared to concede that it can probably be ascertained from various studies that opinion polls do affect public opinion, political or otherwise.
I would like to look at the other side of the coin for a moment. What would happen if this Bill were implemented? This, of course, would not prohibit the use of private polling. That would mean that certain political Parties which have x number of dollars would still be able to commission private polls. They would be able to use the information during the 30-day period to their own advantage.
Much reference has been made to the Toronto area. Let me illustrate one scenario. Under this particular Bill, a poll might be conducted by the Conservative Party which might find out that perhaps the Liberal Party had made a few gains in the Toronto area. Therefore, based on its own private poll, it could innundate the Toronto area with good, solid, Conservative advertising. But would the public be any wiser?
If it were a public poll and all of a sudden we found that the Liberal Party had gained by a certain number of points in the Gallup poll and the Conservatives then innundated the Toronto area with their-I was going to say "propaganda", but let us say advertising, if it were public the discerning person in Toronto could say that is to be expected. This is what the Gallup poll says. And here we have an innundation of the Conservative advertising. So at least this public opinion, the opinion which had been solicited by the public, is at least at a present time still available for the public in general.
I believe that in this day and age more and more people are becoming aware of and alert to the parameters of public opinion polls and how they are conducted. They are, perhaps, a bit more aware of the shortcomings in the way in which these polls are conducted.
It has been mentioned that there is a ban in British Columbia and in certain other parts of the world. I suppose I should ask the question, what is the result of the ban which exists in British Columbia and in other parts of the world? The major political Parties still conduct their own private polls. In accordance with the law, the results are not published. The question I ask is, is the public any wiser in terms of their decisions and in terms of what might still be termed as manipulation on the part of the people who are involved?
In addition to that, I do have some questions about the charter of Rights and the whole question of freedom of the press and freedom of opinion, as mentioned by the previous speaker. Let me just mention some of these concerns. I would be a lot happier if the Liberals would agree, along with the Conservatives, to at least refer this subject matter to committee, because in this short time I cannot underline all of our concerns. If this subject matter were referred to committee we could perhaps bring in some evidence from British Columbia, take a look at the experience in Australia and consider other experience. We could take a look at both sides of the coin. In a short period of time such as we now have available that is certainly not possible.
The Hon. Member indicated the importance of having public information with regard to who does the polling, what are the parameters and what are the statistical methods being used. I noticed he referred to the whole question of random sampling. I am sure the Hon. Member is aware that when we talk about random sampling, it is a statistical technique and method which has been scientifically derived. It is not as the English word would suggest, a "random picking". Those are some of the things which I certainly would like to have taken into consideration. If the Hon. Member had included that type of concern in his Bill, that there be public information available, then this, of course, would be something we could support.
I find it a bit humorous, that the Hon. Member, who speaks so frankly about private enterprise, should today be speaking against these private entrepreneurs who consider all this information private property. All he is really underlining for me is the fact that the whole discussion we have been having, even on the question of property rights, is a little bit broader than what we may have been led to believe.
As to the results of public polls and whether they actually influence an election, the previous speaker referred to the previous election, and that because the people knew there might be a Liberal majority, that did not affect the vote in the west. She underlined a very good point that we should take into consideration, that even the knowledge that the east had gone Liberal did not have an impact on the west. We are fairly independent thinkers out there.
I did want to underline some other concerns, Mr. Speaker. I wish there could have been unanimous consent to have this referred to committee because I would love to see this studied a bit further. I would like to see the Hon. Member come before the committee as a witness to expound a little bit more on this issue. I hope he will not let the issue die.
I know the Commissioner of Official Languages will be bringing forward some recommendations with regard to the Official Languages Act. I hope the Hon. Member, knowing as he does that this Bill will be talked out by the Government, will at least make it a point to send off a representative to the commissioner expressing his concerns. In that way it would be on the public record as something the Commissioner of Official Languages will have to consider, and something which
May 4, 1983

could be brought in for discussion in committee, perhaps as a result of a report and recommendations of the Chief Electoral Officer. I trust the Hon. Member for York-Peel will take my advice and write to the Commissioner so that this is on the public record. Perhaps in that way it might get the airing it deserves in the days ahead.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to share some of these concerns.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to make two or three comments on this particular Bill. It is one of a series brought down by thoughtful Members. You will notice the date on it, May 2, 1980.
There were a number of measures which occurred to me and other thoughtful Members following the election, amendments we felt ought to be made to election procedures. I brought one forward last week in relation to mobile ballot boxes, and I have a number of others. Polling is the matter facing us today.
Permanent electoral polls might have been mentioned. These matters should be brought forward while we are all deeply conscious of the things which come to mind during an election. We cannot discount this subtle influence on voters' minds. The Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) mentioned the ban on the publication of results from the east prior to the closing of polls in the west. That matter is being considered by the committee concerned. There is the very obvious reason for that, because of the influence of the results from the east in the west. Such results can influence favourably or negatively, or they can suggest to people that there is no damn use going out to the polls anyway, so they might as well stay home. That is not good. People should not be influenced in that way. They should be free to express themselves on the candidates and the issues. There is sometimes a desire to get on the bandwagon or defy the bandwagon or, as I say, stay home.
Those people who have spoken so far, particularly on the other side, forget certain things because they live in the centre of this country. They forget that there is a four and one half hour time difference from one side of the country to the other. The results in Newfoundland are known one and one half hours before they are known here. The results in the great metropolitan areas of Ontario and Quebec are known three hours before we close our ballots out on the West Coast.
For the same reason that there should be a ban on the publication of those results, and there is except that they come through via the United States, there should be a ban on influencing voters by means of polls during those last few days. I am not sure whether it should be for 28 days, but on the day an election is called there should be no polls. Individual parties can poll for their own purposes, and that is fine, but they should keep the results to themselves. They know where their soft spots are and what are their issues. They should use the results for their own purposes, not for public purposes.
I fully agree that the Bill should at least go to committee and be considered there.

The Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) specifically referred to the manner in which a poll is conducted and the people who are contacted. He mentioned that if there is a heavy vote turnout, that may throw the poll totally out of whack. The fact is that people who do the polling have a whole series of escape valves available to them. They print it, write about it and discuss it as though it were written or holy rote. In effect they have about eight, nine or ten opportunities to say that if there had been the expected turnout the votes would have gone such and such a way. They might say that no one could have anticipated that there would be such a heavy swell against the leader, or for a leader or whatever the situation might be.
The Hon. Member for York-Peel highlighted some of the great deficiencies in the conducting of polls. He mention professional as opposed to amateurs. I sometimes feel that the amateurs probably do as good a job, if not better, than the professionals because they have a sincere interest in finding answers. One sometimes wonder, when seeing the questions asked in some of these polls across the country from time to time, if the pollster had not already made up his or her mind as to what he or she wanted people to say.
